The use of thermal barrier coatings can increase engine efficiency by permitting increased gas inlet temperatures at present metal temperatures.
TBCs have been successfully tested on several high-pressure turbine (HPT) nozzles and blades.

The TBC system used in this study consists of a low-pressure plasma-sprayed (LPPS) Ni-22Cr-10Al-0.3Y (wt.%) bond coat and a plasma-sprayed yttria partially stabilized zirconia (ZrO2-8%Y2O3) top coat on conventionally cast Rene' 80 alloy substrate.
The bond coat thickness is 0.005 inch ± 0.001 inch, and the zirconia thickness is 0.01 ± 0.002 inch.
Task I focuses on determining the relative importance of various potential failure modes of a plasma-sprayed TBC system.
Task II aims to develop life prediction models for those predominant failure modes determined in Task I.
Task III involves instrumented burner rig testing of TBC-coated Rene' 80 specimens to verify the life model under conditions simulative of turbine blade conditions.
Task V focuses on developing a 'continuum' mechanics life prediction model by applying a structural analysis code.
Task VIII involves developing a comprehensive life prediction model that includes structural analysis, continuum analysis, exceptional failure modes analysis, and fracture mechanics analysis.
Task IX aims to test the dominant features of the comprehensive life prediction model developed in Task VIII.
The program is composed of eight technical tasks.
The study focuses on plasma-sprayed TBC systems and their degradation mechanisms.
The ultimate goal is to create a comprehensive life prediction model for TBCs.
The contract began in April of this year, and work to date has been exclusively in Task I.
